All 36 tests pass. Both files are ready:

- [ttl_cache.py](file:ttl_cache.py) — the `TTLCache` implementation
- [test_ttl_cache.py](file:test_ttl_cache.py) — 36 tests, all passing (`pytest -q` → 36 passed)

**Implementation notes**

- Built on an `OrderedDict` mapping `key → (value, expire_at)`, with least-recently-used first. `get` and `put` both call `move_to_end`, so recency and expiry are tracked independently: expiry is `put_time + ttl` (boundary inclusive, `now >= expire_at` means expired), while `get` only refreshes recency.
- One subtlety worth flagging: because `get` reorders entries by recency but expiry follows last-put time, entry order is **not** expiry order. So purging expired items is a full scan (`_purge_expired`), not an early stop from the LRU end — otherwise a recently-used-but-expired item could shadow an older live one. There's a dedicated test for this (`test_expired_mru_does_not_push_out_live_lru`).
- `put` purges expired entries *before* enforcing capacity, so expired items never push out live ones; `len()` also purges first, so it counts only live items. `capacity == 0` stores nothing (put is a no-op after the purge), and `capacity < 0` / `ttl <= 0` raise `ValueError`.
- The `clock` parameter defaults to `time.monotonic`; tests inject a fake clock for deterministic boundary checks (including the exact `ttl` boundary and fractional TTLs), plus one smoke test against the real clock with a 50 ms TTL.

All 8 reported bugs are fixed in [confparse.py](file:confparse.py), with a test per case in [test_confparse.py](file:test_confparse.py) — all 13 tests pass, plus edge-case checks I ran manually.

**Changes to `parse()`:**

| Reported problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| `;` comments not ignored | Lines starting with `#` **or** `;` are skipped |
| Values with `=` crash | `line.split("=", 1)` — everything after the first `=` is the value |
| Quoted values lose inner spaces | Matching `"…"`/`'…'` wrappers are stripped only after trimming; inner spaces are untouched (`"hello  world"` → `hello  world`) |
| `[Main]` / `[main]` duplicate | Section names lowercased; `data.setdefault(section, {})` merges them |
| Repeated keys | Plain dict assignment — the last value naturally wins |
| Keys before any section crash | `section` starts as `"default"`; the section is created only if such keys exist (no empty `default` otherwise) |
| Indented continuation lines | If a line starts with whitespace and a key was just set, it's appended to that value joined with single spaces |
| Line without `=` | Raises `ValueError: line 3: expected 'key = value', got: 'nonsense'` — 1-based numbering counting all lines, including comments/blanks |

**Edge cases verified beyond the tests:** an indented line with no preceding key is treated as a normal line and errors with its line number; continuations don't leak across a section boundary; unbalanced quotes are kept as-is; a malformed section header like `[oops` also raises a `ValueError` with the line number.

**Result:**

| endpoint | p95_ms | count |

| /api/users | 146.9 | 561 |
| /api/search | 145.2 | 537 |

**How it was computed:**
- From 3000 log lines, filtered out 524 `/health` requests and 301 responses with 5xx status (including 61 `/health` 5xx, which fall under both rules) → 2175 requests kept.
- For each endpoint: sorted the `ms` values, took the value at 1-based position `ceil(0.95·n)` (nearest-rank), formatted to one decimal, and sorted rows by p95 descending.

**Verification:** an independent re-check confirmed the nearest-rank property holds — for every endpoint, exactly ~95.0–95.2% of the kept values are ≤ the reported p95, and the rank index is within bounds.

Done. `business_days` is rewritten and all 9 tests pass.

## What was wrong

The old version looped day by day (`while d < end`), which made century ranges slow, ignored `holidays` entirely, excluded the end date, returned a wrong count (not negated) when `end < start`, and would crash on `datetime` inputs (`datetime + timedelta` works, but `weekday()` comparisons were fine while the loop bound mixed types).

## The fix — [bizdays.py](file:bizdays.py)

- **Both ends included**: range length is `(end - start).days + 1`; count = `5 * (length // 7)` full weeks plus a ≤6-day remainder scan — **O(1)** in range length, no day-by-day loop.
- **Holidays**: collected into a set (duplicates collapse), each holiday subtracted only if it falls inside the range **and** on a weekday — so weekend holidays change nothing, and any iterable (including generators) works.
- **Negative ranges**: `end < start` returns `-business_days(end, start, holidays)` — the same count, negated.
- **Datetimes**: a small `_as_date` helper takes `.date()` from `datetime` instances for `start`, `end` and every holiday entry; only the date part matters.

## Tests — [test_bizdays.py](file:test_bizdays.py)

9 tests, all passing:
- full/partial weeks, single days, both-ends-included cases
- negative ranges (including the symmetric weekend case where `-0 == 0`)
- holidays: weekday, weekend, duplicates, out-of-range, generator input
- datetime inputs for bounds and holidays
- **differential check**: the closed-form result is compared against a naive day-by-day reference for all 7 start weekdays × lengths 0–14, with and without holidays
- **performance**: a 100-year range (verified count: 26090) completes in well under 0.1 s, and 100 years with 1000 holidays still matches the naive reference

One self-correction along the way: I had guessed "26106" for the century count in a comment; the actual verified value is 26090, and the comment now says so.
